records.title: Card Ecosystem & Clearing Architecture
records.description: Overview of the 4-party card payment model in India, dual-message clearing flows, CoFT tokenization rails, and interchange risk boundaries.

sections.what_it_is:
The Indian card payment ecosystem operates predominantly on the international **4-Party Model** (Cardholder, Merchant, Acquirer Bank, and Issuer Bank) facilitated by authorised Card Networks (RuPay, Visa, Mastercard, American Express). Transactions route through two distinct operational messages: **Dual-Message System (DMS)**, separating real-time authorization holds from batch settlement, or **Single-Message System (SMS)**, common in ATM cash withdrawals and PIN-based debit POS.

Under Reserve Bank of India (RBI) mandates, all domestic Card-Not-Present (CNP) e-commerce transactions require **Card-on-File Tokenisation (CoFT)**, barring merchants and payment aggregators from storing 16-digit Primary Account Numbers (PAN), and **Additional Factor of Authentication (AFA)** with at least one dynamic authentication factor.

```
┌────────────┐               ┌────────────────────┐               ┌─────────────┐
│ Cardholder │──(Presents)──►│ Merchant / Web / PA│──(Auth Req)──►│Acquirer Bank│
└────────────┘               └────────────────────┘               └──────┬──────┘
                                                                         │
                                                                         ▼
┌────────────┐               ┌────────────────────┐               ┌─────────────┐
│Issuer Bank │◄──(Auth Req)──│    Card Network    │◄──(Routes)────│Payment Switch
└─────┬──────┘               │(RuPay/Visa/MC/Amex)│               └─────────────┘
      │                      └────────────────────┘
      ▼
(Verifies Balance, Limit, AFA & Token Cryptogram)
```

---
sections.impact:
- **Cardholders:** Subject to unauthorized billing, card-not-present fraud, hidden subscription recurring debits, and ATM cloning if chip-and-PIN fallbacks are misconfigured.
- **Issuers & Acquirers:** Exposure to chargeback dispute liability, cross-border fraud losses, interchange settlement risk, and regulatory compensation penalties (₹100/day under RBI Harmonisation of TAT) for delayed dispute credits.
- **Ecosystem:** Settlement gridlock when merchant acquirers or payment aggregators suffer escrow reconciliation breaks between batch clearing files and network net settlement statements.

---
sections.common_patterns:
### Pattern 1: Dual-Message Authorization vs. Presentment Discrepancy
In e-commerce and hotel/fuel pre-authorizations, the issuer places a temporary hold on the cardholder's credit limit or available balance during authorization (`Auth`). If the merchant does not capture or submit the clearing presentment file within the validity window (typically 5 to 7 days), the hold expires, yet delayed presentment files may force settlement debits unexpectedly, triggering customer disputes.

### Pattern 2: Card-on-File Tokenization (CoFT) De-tokenization Mismatch
Merchants invoke tokenized checkouts where a cryptographic token replaces the PAN. The payment aggregator routes the token to the Card Network Token Service Provider (TSP). If the TSP cryptogram fails validation (e.g. timestamp skew, domain restriction mismatch), the transaction is rejected without exposing cardholder PANs.

### Pattern 3: International Card-Not-Present (CNP) 2FA Bypass
Domestic transactions strictly enforce RBI AFA (2FA OTP/biometrics). However, foreign merchants routing through offshore acquirers outside India may initiate transactions via 1-factor paths (card number + expiry + CVV), bypassing OTP and creating cross-border chargeback exposure unless international limits are disabled by default.

---
sections.what_to_do: | Basis | Owner | Action | |---|---|---| | **RBI Master Direction (2022)** [1] | **Issuer bank** | Implement mandate controls allowing cardholders to dynamically toggle and set custom limits for domestic/international, online (CNP), POS (CP), and contactless ATM transactions via mobile banking. | | **RBI CoFT Mandate** [2] | **Payment aggregator & Merchant** | Purge stored plain PAN/CVV records from merchant databases; use network-issued tokens for recurring and express checkout flows with explicit cardholder consent. | | **RBI AFA Directions (2025)** [3] | **Issuer bank** | Enforce a minimum of two distinct authentication factors for all domestic digital payment transactions, with at least one factor being dynamically generated. | | **RBI TAT & Compensation** [4] | **Acquirer & Issuer bank** | Auto-reverse failed POS/e-commerce transactions within `T+5` days; pay proactive compensation of ₹100/day for each day of delay beyond `T+5`. | | **Atlas Guidance** | **Risk ops & Fraud engines** | Monitor card velocity bursts (e.g. 5 transactions within 60 seconds across distinct merchant categories) to flag automated BIN brute-force probing. | ---
sections.watch_outs:
- **Legitimate Pre-auth Holds vs. Unauthorized Debits:** Car rentals and hotels place large pre-authorizations. Customer service teams must verify whether a pending debit is an authorization hold or a settled presentment before filing unauthorized electronic transaction claims under RBI rules.
- **Contactless Tap-and-Pay Limits:** Under RBI directions, offline contactless transactions up to ₹5,000 are exempt from AFA PIN entry, requiring issuers to maintain aggressive aggregate daily velocity thresholds to limit physical card theft exposure.
- **Testing Method:** Validate CoFT failure handling in staging by injecting expired cryptograms, invalid token domain restrictions, and simulated issuer timeouts to verify that payment gateways fail closed without falling back to plain-text PAN storage.

records.fullMarkdown: --- title: Card Ecosystem & Clearing Architecture description: Overview of the 4-party card payment model in India, dual-message clearing flows, CoFT tokenization rails, and interchange risk boundaries. recordId: CARD-OVERVIEW recordType: explainer products: - cards theme: overview lifecycle: - processing - settlement actors: - cardholder - merchant - acquirer-bank - issuer-bank - card-network - payment-aggregator evidenceLayers: - official - industry - atlas lastSourceCheck: "2026-11-25" reviewStage: source-checked --- ## What it is The Indian card payment ecosystem operates predominantly on the international **4-Party Model** (Cardholder, Merchant, Acquirer Bank, and Issuer Bank) facilitated by authorised Card Networks (RuPay, Visa, Mastercard, American Express). Transactions route through two distinct operational messages: **Dual-Message System (DMS)**, separating real-time authorization holds from batch settlement, or **Single-Message System (SMS)**, common in ATM cash withdrawals and PIN-based debit POS. Under Reserve Bank of India (RBI) mandates, all domestic Card-Not-Present (CNP) e-commerce transactions require **Card-on-File Tokenisation (CoFT)**, barring merchants and payment aggregators from storing 16-digit Primary Account Numbers (PAN), and **Additional Factor of Authentication (AFA)** with at least one dynamic authentication factor. ``` ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ │ Cardholder │──(Presents)──►│ Merchant / Web / PA│──(Auth Req)──►│Acquirer Bank│ └────────────┘ └────────────────────┘ └──────┬──────┘ │ ▼ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ │Issuer Bank │◄──(Auth Req)──│ Card Network │◄──(Routes)────│Payment Switch └─────┬──────┘ │(RuPay/Visa/MC/Amex)│ └─────────────┘ │ └────────────────────┘ ▼ (Verifies Balance, Limit, AFA & Token Cryptogram) ``` --- ## Impact - **Cardholders:** Subject to unauthorized billing, card-not-present fraud, hidden subscription recurring debits, and ATM cloning if chip-and-PIN fallbacks are misconfigured. - **Issuers & Acquirers:** Exposure to chargeback dispute liability, cross-border fraud losses, interchange settlement risk, and regulatory compensation penalties (₹100/day under RBI Harmonisation of TAT) for delayed dispute credits. - **Ecosystem:** Settlement gridlock when merchant acquirers or payment aggregators suffer escrow reconciliation breaks between batch clearing files and network net settlement statements. --- ## Common patterns ### Pattern 1: Dual-Message Authorization vs. Presentment Discrepancy In e-commerce and hotel/fuel pre-authorizations, the issuer places a temporary hold on the cardholder's credit limit or available balance during authorization (`Auth`). If the merchant does not capture or submit the clearing presentment file within the validity window (typically 5 to 7 days), the hold expires, yet delayed presentment files may force settlement debits unexpectedly, triggering customer disputes. ### Pattern 2: Card-on-File Tokenization (CoFT) De-tokenization Mismatch Merchants invoke tokenized checkouts where a cryptographic token replaces the PAN. The payment aggregator routes the token to the Card Network Token Service Provider (TSP). If the TSP cryptogram fails validation (e.g. timestamp skew, domain restriction mismatch), the transaction is rejected without exposing cardholder PANs. ### Pattern 3: International Card-Not-Present (CNP) 2FA Bypass Domestic transactions strictly enforce RBI AFA (2FA OTP/biometrics). However, foreign merchants routing through offshore acquirers outside India may initiate transactions via 1-factor paths (card number + expiry + CVV), bypassing OTP and creating cross-border chargeback exposure unless international limits are disabled by default. --- ## What to do | Basis | Owner | Action | |---|---|---| | **RBI Master Direction (2022)** [1] | **Issuer bank** | Implement mandate controls allowing cardholders to dynamically toggle and set custom limits for domestic/international, online (CNP), POS (CP), and contactless ATM transactions via mobile banking. | | **RBI CoFT Mandate** [2] | **Payment aggregator & Merchant** | Purge stored plain PAN/CVV records from merchant databases; use network-issued tokens for recurring and express checkout flows with explicit cardholder consent. | | **RBI AFA Directions (2025)** [3] | **Issuer bank** | Enforce a minimum of two distinct authentication factors for all domestic digital payment transactions, with at least one factor being dynamically generated. | | **RBI TAT & Compensation** [4] | **Acquirer & Issuer bank** | Auto-reverse failed POS/e-commerce transactions within `T+5` days; pay proactive compensation of ₹100/day for each day of delay beyond `T+5`. | | **Atlas Guidance** | **Risk ops & Fraud engines** | Monitor card velocity bursts (e.g. 5 transactions within 60 seconds across distinct merchant categories) to flag automated BIN brute-force probing. | --- ## Watch-outs and validation - **Legitimate Pre-auth Holds vs. Unauthorized Debits:** Car rentals and hotels place large pre-authorizations. Customer service teams must verify whether a pending debit is an authorization hold or a settled presentment before filing unauthorized electronic transaction claims under RBI rules. - **Contactless Tap-and-Pay Limits:** Under RBI directions, offline contactless transactions up to ₹5,000 are exempt from AFA PIN entry, requiring issuers to maintain aggressive aggregate daily velocity thresholds to limit physical card theft exposure. - **Testing Method:** Validate CoFT failure handling in staging by injecting expired cryptograms, invalid token domain restrictions, and simulated issuer timeouts to verify that payment gateways fail closed without falling back to plain-text PAN storage. --- ## References and review history 1. **RBI Master Direction – Credit Card and Debit Card – Issuance and Conduct Directions, 2022** (`RBI/DoS/2022-23/92`, updated 2024/2026). records.description: UPI-001 — account-level outbound burst and rapid balance-depletion signals.

sections.what_it_is: Detects sudden bursts of outgoing UPI payments—such as multiple back-to-back transfers to unfamiliar payees, rapid splitting right after an incoming credit, or abrupt balance draining—early enough to flag account takeover, scam coercion, or mule cash-outs. Outbound velocity is a **risk signal, not standalone proof of fraud**.
sections.impact:
- **Customer:** Victim balances or compromised accounts are drained across multiple rapid hops before alerts are reviewed.
- **Banks & PSPs:** Counting raw transfers without comparing against the customer's own baseline misses stealth draining or floods queues with noisy retail alerts.
sections.common_patterns:
- Multiple outbound UPI debits or new beneficiary additions compressed into a short window.
- First-time mobile/UPI channel usage on an established account, or excessive burst activity right after account opening.
- Outbound bursts immediately following a new device link or an unfamiliar large credit.

*(For program-wide EFRM governance, staffing, and alert-tuning obligations, see [Transaction velocity and EFRM monitoring](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/transaction-velocity/).)*
sections.what_to_do:
| Basis | Owner | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory | Commercial, Payments & Small Finance banks | Parameterize monitoring alerts for transaction velocity (electronic fund transfers and new beneficiary additions in short periods), first-time mobile/internet channel usage, and excessive new-account activity. RBI sets no fixed rupee/count cutoff—banks document risk-based limits. |
| Regulatory | Non-bank PSOs | Maintain real-time/near-real-time fraud monitoring and facilitate online participant alerts for velocity and new-account spikes (effective immediately for Large/Medium PSOs; Apr 1, 2028 for Small PSOs). |
| Research & academic | Risk & ML teams | An Indian RBIH NFPC study found alternating high-velocity outbound runs paired with prior inflows and dormancy separated mules from legitimate bursts that revert quickly to baseline. |
| Research & academic | Fraud product teams | An empirical GPay India evaluation achieving >88% recall saw ~30% precision on evaluated splits—meaning behavioral velocity triggers alone create too many false blocks if wired directly to hard freezes without step-up or review. |
| Atlas guidance | Remitter banks, PSPs, TPAPs | Score rolling 15-minute, 1-hour, and 24-hour outbound counts, value, balance depletion share, and unique-new-payee ratio relative to each account's own 30/90-day baseline; prioritize bursts paired with recent device binding or unfamiliar inflows. |
sections.watch_outs:
- **Legitimate lookalikes:** Small merchants paying suppliers at day-end, festive shopping/gifting, group-trip splits, salary-day family transfers, and active new users. Prefer step-up confirmation or scoped temporary holds over blanket account freezes.
- **Signals needed:** Timestamps, debit/credit direction, outcome status, amount, pre/post balance, anonymized counterparty VPA/account ID, account tenure, and device/session context.
- **How to validate:** Measure alert `precision@k` at your real daily analyst queue capacity, track false-positive overturn rates by segment (merchant vs retail), and stress-test against salary-week and festival spikes.

records.description: UPI-002 — pass-through layering networks, RBIH MuleHunter.AI / I4C coordination, and relational detection limits.

sections.what_it_is: Money mules receive fraud proceeds from unrelated victims and quickly forward them onward across other bank accounts, wallets, or cash-outs. On its own, each UPI transaction can look like normal retail spend—the giveaway is **tight inflow-to-outflow coupling, sudden activity after dormancy, and shared infrastructure** (devices, addresses, IP/branch attributes) tying separate accounts together.
sections.impact:
- **Beneficiary & remitter banks:** High alert backlogs, NCRP lien/freeze coordination overhead, and regulatory scrutiny on mule onboarding.
- **Innocent sellers & community accounts:** Broad or blunt freezes lock up legitimate livelihoods when normal merchants receive a tainted scam transfer.
- **Ecosystem recovery:** Every extra hop delays inter-bank tracing and lowers funds recoverable after fraud reporting.
sections.common_patterns:
- **Dormant-to-burst pass-through:** A low-balance or inactive account receives multiple inbound credits and immediately drains onward.
- **Shared-entity mule rings:** Separate customer accounts reuse underlying phone numbers, addresses, postal PINs, counterparties, or devices.
- **Layered cross-rail cash-out:** Inbound UPI credits rapidly scatter across linked UPI handles, cards, or ATM withdrawals.
sections.what_to_do:
| Basis | Owner | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory | Commercial, Payments & Small Finance banks | Monitor new-account activity spikes, rapid velocity, beneficiary additions, and transfers to VPAs/mobile numbers linked to recorded frauds; maintain stakeholder coordination SOPs. |
| Regulatory | Commercial, Payments & Small Finance banks | Run Data Analytics/MI digital transaction monitoring and EWS frameworks; follow natural-justice due process (21-day Show Cause Notice and reasoned order) before formal fraud classification. |
| Regulatory | Banks, I4C, RBIH | Coordinate NCRP Suspect Registry intelligence with RBIH `MuleHunter.AI`; RBI's Apr 2026 discussion paper also consults on monitoring credits against KYC profile (non-binding). |
| Research & academic | Risk & ML teams | On the Indian RBIH NFPC dataset (~237.8M txns across 96,091 accounts), GBDTs (`XGBoost`/`LightGBM`) achieved 96–99% precision for tiny daily queues (`k=100`), whereas temporal heterogeneous GNNs outperformed GBDTs at deeper queues (`k=500`) by capturing 2-to-4-hop shared counterparties, addresses, and PINs. |
| Research & academic | Investigation teams | An OCBC Singapore study combined 280 account features, LightGBM, TreeSHAP, and constrained LLM case narratives to lift investigator alert yield from 61% to 89% (non-India AML comparison; dataset limits apply). |
| Atlas guidance | Banks, PAs | Score inflow/outflow ratio, onward-debit latency, fan-in/fan-out diversity, and shared device/address attributes; isolate only contested funds where permitted instead of freezing entire livelihood accounts blindly. |
sections.watch_outs:
- **Legitimate lookalikes:** Community or housing-society collections, micro-merchants/kiranas, gig-worker payouts, and innocent sellers who unwittingly accepted payment from a scam victim.
- **Positive-unlabelled feedback trap:** Treating every uninvestigated account as "confirmed clean" teaches models to treat undetected mule rings as normal behavior.
- **Signals needed:** KYC profile/account age, credit-debit latency pairs, anonymized counterparty graph edges, shared contact/address indicators, NCRP Suspect Registry hits, and investigator dispositions.
- **How to validate:** Enforce strict per-account time cutoffs (`τ(v) <= t_seed`) to stop future label leakage, evaluate `precision@k` at your real daily analyst queue size, and audit overturned freezes separately from confirmed fraud.

## What it is
Money mules receive fraud proceeds from unrelated victims and quickly forward them onward across other bank accounts, wallets, or cash-outs. On its own, each UPI transaction can look like normal retail spend—the giveaway is **tight inflow-to-outflow coupling, sudden activity after dormancy, and shared infrastructure** (devices, addresses, IP/branch attributes) tying separate accounts together.

## Impact
- **Beneficiary & remitter banks:** High alert backlogs, NCRP lien/freeze coordination overhead, and regulatory scrutiny on mule onboarding.
- **Innocent sellers & community accounts:** Broad or blunt freezes lock up legitimate livelihoods when normal merchants receive a tainted scam transfer.
- **Ecosystem recovery:** Every extra hop delays inter-bank tracing and lowers funds recoverable after fraud reporting.

## Common patterns
- **Dormant-to-burst pass-through:** A low-balance or inactive account receives multiple inbound credits and immediately drains onward.
- **Shared-entity mule rings:** Separate customer accounts reuse underlying phone numbers, addresses, postal PINs, counterparties, or devices.
- **Layered cross-rail cash-out:** Inbound UPI credits rapidly scatter across linked UPI handles, cards, or ATM withdrawals.

| Basis | Owner | Action |
|---|---|---|

- **Legitimate lookalikes:** Community or housing-society collections, micro-merchants/kiranas, gig-worker payouts, and innocent sellers who unwittingly accepted payment from a scam victim.

sections.what_it_is: Account takeover (ATO) happens when an attacker steals control of a customer's mobile number, SIM, UPI app login, or credentials and uses that access to drain the account. While bank device checks have reduced pure technical takeovers relative to manipulation scams, silent SIM swaps, recycled mobile numbers, and malware-based re-registration still create high-speed losses.
sections.impact:
- **Customer:** Rapid unauthorized transfers shortly after a SIM swap, device switch, or mobile-number change.
- **Bank & PSP:** Sudden shift from trusted-device activity to risky transfers and zero-warning dispute liability checks.
- **Legitimate users:** Overly rigid device checks after genuine phone upgrades, lost SIM replacements, or travel can lock victims out during emergencies.
sections.common_patterns:
- **SIM swap & silent re-binding:** Attackers transfer the victim's mobile number to a new SIM and re-register UPI on an unfamiliar handset.
- **Recycled or disconnected mobile numbers:** Reassigned MSISDNs expose dormant accounts or linked VPAs if telecom revocation lists are not checked.
- **Post-change draining:** Credentials or phone numbers are updated and followed immediately by high-value or first-time-channel payouts.
sections.what_to_do:
| Basis | Owner | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory | Commercial, Payments & Small Finance banks | Bind mobile apps to hardware, software, and service identifiers; require re-auth at launch and after inactivity; block access when remote-access apps are detected; monitor first-time channel, IP, geo, and behavioral anomalies. |
| Regulatory | Non-bank PSOs | Enforce binding tied to both device and SIM (with re-binding after prolonged disuse), plus a minimum 12-hour cooling period for online payments after any mobile-number or email change. |
| Atlas guidance | Banks, TPAPs, PSPs | Screen customer mobile numbers against the DoT Mobile Number Revocation List (MNRL) to catch disconnected or reassigned numbers early. |
| Atlas guidance | Banks, TPAPs | Send instant out-of-band alerts on new device linkages, and apply step-up checks when a newly bound device attempts immediate high-value transfers. |

sections.what_it_is: A scammer sends a UPI payment request and tricks the victim into thinking that approving the popup and entering their UPI PIN will *credit* money into their account. Because authorization prompts can look routine when someone is rushed or coached on a call, victims unknowingly approve money *leaving* their account.
sections.impact:
- **Customer:** Immediate, real-time debit that the victim authorized under deception, leading to disputed recovery.
- **Bank & PSP:** High APP-scam complaint load and regulatory liability exposure where clear, specific scam warnings were missing.
- **Merchant & App:** Legitimate merchant pull checkouts lose trust and conversion when users fear collect popups.
sections.common_patterns:
- **Fake marketplace buyer:** A buyer pretends to send payment for a listed item and instead sends a collect request.
- **Fake refund or prize:** A caller tells the customer to approve a pending prompt and enter their UPI PIN to receive cashback or a refund.
- **Urgency coaching:** The scammer stays on the line rushing the victim past the screen before they check payment direction.
sections.what_to_do:
| Basis | Owner | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory | Banks, PSPs, Apps | Discontinue all Person-to-Person (P2P) UPI Collect requests (banned beyond Oct 1, 2025). Keep only Merchant (P2M) collect flows active. |
| Regulatory | Commercial banks | Treat deception- or coercion-induced approvals as fraudulent transactions (effective Jan 1, 2027), and record whether directed scam warnings were shown and ignored. |
| Industry practice | Merchants, PAs | Favor app-to-app UPI Intent over Collect in mobile checkouts; keep P2M Collect and Dynamic QR mostly for desktop checkouts and exempted flows such as IPO mandates. |
| Atlas guidance | PSPs, Issuer banks | Enforce P2P collect blocks at the switch and PSP layers, and verify merchant MID/MCC records before routing any pull request. |
| Atlas guidance | UPI Apps, Banks | Show unmistakable debit framing ("Paying Rs X to verified merchant — money leaves your account") with higher-friction warnings on unusual collect prompts. |

- **Signals needed:** Initiation channel (`P2P` vs `P2M` collect vs `intent`), payee VPA/MID/MCC, payer-payee prior history, device/app context, and notification timing.
- **How to validate:** Run negative switch tests confirming P2P collect requests fail cleanly, test user comprehension of debit-direction screens, and track drop-off vs. scam loss when warnings trigger.

## What it is
A scammer sends a UPI payment request and tricks the victim into thinking that approving the popup and entering their UPI PIN will *credit* money into their account. Because authorization prompts can look routine when someone is rushed or coached on a call, victims unknowingly approve money *leaving* their account.

## Impact
- **Customer:** Immediate, real-time debit that the victim authorized under deception, leading to disputed recovery.
- **Bank & PSP:** High APP-scam complaint load and regulatory liability exposure where clear, specific scam warnings were missing.
- **Merchant & App:** Legitimate merchant pull checkouts lose trust and conversion when users fear collect popups.

## Common patterns
- **Fake marketplace buyer:** A buyer pretends to send payment for a listed item and instead sends a collect request.
- **Fake refund or prize:** A caller tells the customer to approve a pending prompt and enter their UPI PIN to receive cashback or a refund.
- **Urgency coaching:** The scammer stays on the line rushing the victim past the screen before they check payment direction.

## What to do (rules and mitigations)

| Basis | Owner | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory | Banks, PSPs, Apps | Discontinue all Person-to-Person (P2P) UPI Collect requests (banned beyond Oct 1, 2025). Keep only Merchant (P2M) collect flows active. |
| Regulatory | Commercial banks | Treat deception- or coercion-induced approvals as fraudulent transactions (effective Jan 1, 2027), and record whether directed scam warnings were shown and ignored. |

| Atlas guidance | UPI Apps, Banks | Show unmistakable debit framing ("Paying Rs X to verified merchant — money leaves your account") with higher-friction warnings on unusual collect prompts. |

- **Legitimate lookalikes:** Desktop e-commerce checkouts, recurring utility or subscription bills, and IPO ASBA-via-UPI mandates where the payer expects a pull request.
- **Signals needed:** Initiation channel (`P2P` vs `P2M` collect vs `intent`), payee VPA/MID/MCC, payer-payee prior history, device/app context, and notification timing.

records.description: UPI-005 — merchant/PA payment status, webhook authenticity, idempotency, and order-fulfilment reconciliation.

sections.what_it_is: In online UPI merchant checkouts, the customer's browser screen, redirect `callback_url`, asynchronous Payment Aggregator (PA) webhook, and bank settlement file are four separate states. Order fulfillment breaks when merchants trust unverified browser redirects, process retried webhooks as second payments, leave orders permanently stuck in `PENDING`, or send duplicate refunds. *(For interbank settlement-file matching and `T+1`/`T+5` reversal SLAs, see [Settlement and reconciliation exceptions](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/settlement-exceptions/).)*
sections.impact:
- **Customer:** Account gets debited while the order stays failed or cancelled, locking funds until `T+5` auto-reversal or manual refund.
- **Merchant:** Double shipment of goods or duplicate payouts when retried webhooks are not deduplicated.
- **PA & Acquirer:** Unmatched order vs escrow records violate PA payout transparency and refund rules.
sections.common_patterns:
- **Browser callback spoofing / drop-off:** Customer closes the browser before redirect returns, or an attacker spoofs query parameters on an unverified `callback_url`.
- **Duplicate / out-of-order webhooks:** At-least-once delivery or `order.paid` arriving before `payment.captured` triggers double fulfillment or false state regressions.
- **Stuck `PENDING` auto-cancellation:** Premature cron job cancels a paid order whose webhook arrived slow, causing support complaints.
sections.what_to_do:
| Basis | Owner | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory | Payment Aggregators, Merchants, Acquirers | Define clear failed-transaction and refund terms in PA/merchant/acquirer agreements; settle merchant balances transparently with day-end escrow adequacy, and route refunds/reversals through escrow unless merchant-managed with payer clarity. |

## What it is
Fraudsters share QR codes or payment links promising cashbacks, refunds, prizes, or advance payments. Scanning the QR or tapping the link pre-fills an **outgoing payment** to an attacker-controlled VPA or merchant, so victims who enter their UPI PIN thinking they are "claiming" money authorize a debit instead. - **Customer:** Instant unauthorized-looking loss even though the victim entered their PIN, creating complex dispute cases.

sections.what_it_is: Ensures payment approvals genuinely come from the authorized customer and bound device rather than replayed credentials, stolen static passwords, or man-in-the-middle (MITM) tampering—while keeping exempted fast flows (like recurring mandates and Tap-and-Pay NFC UPI) correctly scoped.
sections.impact:
- **Customer & Issuer:** Stolen static credentials or intercepted sessions let attackers authorize debits without clear merchant confirmation on alerts or OTPs.
- **Product teams:** Misreading RBI exemptions causes either broken checkout flows or non-compliant skip-auth bugs.
sections.common_patterns:
- Every domestic digital payment authorization unless explicitly covered by an active RBI two-factor exemption.
- High-risk sessions showing new geo, velocity, or payee changes suited for adaptive authentication.
- Mobile/web handshakes prone to TLS/session tampering.
sections.what_to_do: | Basis | Owner | Action | |---|---|---| | Regulatory | Payment System Providers & Participants | Require at least two distinct authentication factors per transaction, including at least one dynamically generated/proven factor for non-card-present payments; recognize active exemptions (e.g., subsequent recurring e-mandates and NFC Tap-and-Pay UPI on POS). Issuers bear responsibility for compliance and may apply risk-based checks. | | Regulatory | Commercial, Payments & Small Finance banks | Implement phishing/keylogger-resistant MFA, optional risk-based adaptive auth, SMS/email alerts for transactions and new linkages showing the actual merchant name (not only the PA), and MITM controls terminating interfered sessions. | | Regulatory | Non-bank PSOs | Place OTP codes (where used) at the end of messages alongside the specific transaction reference, and preserve intact session security and encryption across mobile channels. | | Regulatory | UPI apps and PSP banks offering additional authentication | NPCI OC-226 allows customers to opt into Aadhaar face authentication for PIN setup or reset, and on-device biometrics as an alternative to the PIN for payments. Check device compatibility and security, obtain explicit consent with an opt-out, and renew consent after device binding before allowing further biometric payments. [4] | | Regulatory | Issuer banks offering additional authentication | Verify customer eligibility and credentials before enabling biometrics or authorizing PIN setup or reset. If a UPI PIN changes or is reset, disable the biometric payment method for that account across UPI apps until fresh consent. [4] | | Atlas guidance | TPAPs, Remitter banks, PSPs | Cryptographically bind UPI PIN and device factor proofs to the exact amount, payee VPA/MID, and session integrity; terminate transactions immediately on TLS pinning or runtime tamper failures. |
sections.watch_outs: - **Legitimate lookalikes:** Exempted low-value NFC Tap-and-Pay UPI transactions, subsequent recurring e-mandate debits, and adaptive step-ups during genuine cross-city travel. Avoid dropping valid sessions solely on transient weak cellular handoffs. - **Signals needed:** Auth factors verified (`PIN`, biometric, device token, exempt mandate/NFC), session TLS/pinning telemetry, merchant descriptor fields, and risk-based step-up audit logs. - **How to validate:** Audit `Annexure-1` exemption flags against live product behavior, verify TLS error termination, and inspect live SMS/OTP alert templates for merchant-name display and end-placed OTP format. - **Biometric rollout scope:** OC-226 initially capped on-device biometric payments at ₹5,000 per transaction. Check the current NPCI implementation documents and any later circulars before using that amount as a production limit. [4]

sections.impact:
- **Security exposure:** Unlimited retries allow automated probing or stolen-device guessing until an account compromises.
- **Customer friction:** Treating switch timeouts or connectivity errors like wrong-PIN attacks locks legitimate users out during urgent payments.
sections.common_patterns:
- Sequential wrong UPI PIN, invalid OTP, or failed mobile-app login attempts inside a short time window.
- Failed-auth spikes paired with unfamiliar devices, new VPAs, or IP changes.
- Reactivation flows after temporary security lockouts.
sections.what_to_do:

|---|---|---|

sections.what_it_is: Defines who bears the loss, what deadlines apply, and what proof banks must keep when a customer suffers an **unauthorized transaction** or an **approved-under-deception fraud**—separating these recovery rules from technical failed-payment reversals (`T+1`/`T+5`).
sections.impact:
- **Customers:** Blurring bank deficiency or third-party breaches into customer negligence wrongly shifts losses onto victims, or delays shadow/value-dated reversals.
- **Banks:** Rejecting claims without documented evidence or failing to halt transfers immediately after a fraud report shifts full post-reporting liability onto the bank (with the **burden of proof resting on the bank**).
sections.common_patterns:
- **Commercial Banks (effective Jan 1, 2027):** Covers transactions on or after Jan 1, 2027 (`RBI/2026-27/167`, *excluding* SFBs, PBs, RRBs, and LABs), covering both unauthorized EBTs and coercion/deception-induced *Fraudulent EBTs*.
- **Payments Banks & baseline circular (`RBI/2017-18/15`):** Retains the existing 3-working-day zero-liability, 4–7 working-day cap, 10-working-day shadow-reversal, and 90-day resolution timeline where bank-class replacement has not taken effect.
sections.what_to_do:
| Basis | Owner | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory | Commercial banks (EBTs >= Jan 1, 2027) | Send free SMS/email alerts (EBTs > ₹500) with an SMS-reply objection number, provide 24x7 reporting links, advise NCRP/1930 filing, log all timestamps, acknowledge immediately, and halt further debits upon report. |
| Regulatory | Commercial banks (EBTs >= Jan 1, 2027) | Bear the **burden of proving customer liability**; guarantee zero liability for bank negligence and for third-party breaches reported within **5 calendar days**; bear all post-report losses; issue value-dated reversals and give written reasons for any claim rejection. |
| Regulatory | Commercial banks (EBTs >= Jan 1, 2027) | Administer the one-year small-value fraud compensation scheme for individuals/sole proprietors (gross loss <= ₹50,000 reported to **both NCRP/1930 and bank within 5 calendar days** under negligence cases): pay **85% of net loss up to ₹25,000** within 5 calendar days of completed claim (shared RBI 65%, issuer bank 10%, beneficiary bank 10% below ₹29,412; ₹19,118 / ₹2,941 / ₹2,941 up to ₹50,000). |
| Regulatory | Payments Banks & pre-2027 baseline SCBs/SFBs/RRBs | Apply **3 working days** zero liability, **4–7 working days** capped liability, **10 working days** shadow reversal, and **90 days** final resolution under the existing baseline directions. |
| Atlas guidance | Banks, Fraud ops | Build evidence-preserving intake pipelines recording alert delivery timestamps, SMS-reply blocks, directed scam-warning impressions, auth/device logs, and NCRP reference numbers from intake. |
sections.watch_outs:
- **False or repeat claims vs unfair rejections:** Screen against statutory repeat/false-claim declarations while ensuring legitimate third-party breaches or missing-warning cases are not defaulted to "customer negligence" without documented proof.
- **Signals needed:** SMS/email/push delivery receipts, customer reporting timestamps, NCRP/1930 ticket IDs, authentication/device logs, directed warning impression logs, and written rejection records.
- **How to validate:** Test 24x7 SMS-reply freeze speed, verify immutable timestamp logging, and audit sample rejected liability claims against bank burden-of-proof criteria.

## What it solves
Defines who bears the loss, what deadlines apply, and what proof banks must keep when a customer suffers an **unauthorized transaction** or an **approved-under-deception fraud**—separating these recovery rules from technical failed-payment reversals (`T+1`/`T+5`).

## Impact when mishandled
- **Customers:** Blurring bank deficiency or third-party breaches into customer negligence wrongly shifts losses onto victims, or delays shadow/value-dated reversals.
- **Banks:** Rejecting claims without documented evidence or failing to halt transfers immediately after a fraud report shifts full post-reporting liability onto the bank (with the **burden of proof resting on the bank**).

## Where it applies
- **Commercial Banks (effective Jan 1, 2027):** Covers transactions on or after Jan 1, 2027 (`RBI/2026-27/167`, *excluding* SFBs, PBs, RRBs, and LABs), covering both unauthorized EBTs and coercion/deception-induced *Fraudulent EBTs*.
- **Payments Banks & baseline circular (`RBI/2017-18/15`):** Retains the existing 3-working-day zero-liability, 4–7 working-day cap, 10-working-day shadow-reversal, and 90-day resolution timeline where bank-class replacement has not taken effect.

## What to do (rules and workflows)

| Basis | Owner | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory | Commercial banks (EBTs >= Jan 1, 2027) | Send free SMS/email alerts (EBTs > ₹500) with an SMS-reply objection number, provide 24x7 reporting links, advise NCRP/1930 filing, log all timestamps, acknowledge immediately, and halt further debits upon report. |
| Regulatory | Commercial banks (EBTs >= Jan 1, 2027) | Bear the **burden of proving customer liability**; guarantee zero liability for bank negligence and for third-party breaches reported within **5 calendar days**; bear all post-report losses; issue value-dated reversals and give written reasons for any claim rejection. |
| Regulatory | Commercial banks (EBTs >= Jan 1, 2027) | Administer the one-year small-value fraud compensation scheme for individuals/sole proprietors (gross loss <= ₹50,000 reported to **both NCRP/1930 and bank within 5 calendar days** under negligence cases): pay **85% of net loss up to ₹25,000** within 5 calendar days of completed claim (shared RBI 65%, issuer bank 10%, beneficiary bank 10% below ₹29,412; ₹19,118 / ₹2,941 / ₹2,941 up to ₹50,000). |
| Regulatory | Payments Banks & pre-2027 baseline SCBs/SFBs/RRBs | Apply **3 working days** zero liability, **4–7 working days** capped liability, **10 working days** shadow reversal, and **90 days** final resolution under the existing baseline directions. |

## Watch-outs and validation
- **False or repeat claims vs unfair rejections:** Screen against statutory repeat/false-claim declarations while ensuring legitimate third-party breaches or missing-warning cases are not defaulted to "customer negligence" without documented proof.
- **Signals needed:** SMS/email/push delivery receipts, customer reporting timestamps, NCRP/1930 ticket IDs, authentication/device logs, directed warning impression logs, and written rejection records.

## What it covers
On April 9, 2026, RBI issued *Discussion Paper – Exploring safeguards in digital payments to curb frauds* (comments closed May 8, 2026). **This is a non-binding consultation paper—none of its suggested thresholds or options is enacted law unless RBI subsequently issues formal directions.**

## Why it matters
- **Shifting fraud mix:** RBI notes that technical account takeovers have declined relative to **Authorised Push Payment (APP)** scams driven by social engineering, bogus call centres, impersonation, and mule networks targeting NCRP.
- **Current ecosystem tools cited:** Notes Digital Payment Security Controls, DoT's **Mobile Number Revocation List (MNRL)** on DIP, I4C's NCRP SOP, and RBIH's `MuleHunter.AI` (2024).

## Key proposals and trade-offs

| Basis | Focus area | Proposed option & trade-offs |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory *(consultation)* | **Option 1 — Lagged credit** | Floats a 1-hour payer-bank delay (provisional debit with payer cancellation window) for non-merchant, non-recurring APP transfers above a suggested **₹10,000** limit (excluding whitelisted payees) to break "golden hour" coercion. RBI notes this conflicts with real-time UX expectations and attackers may coach victims to whitelist payees. |
| Regulatory *(consultation)* | **Option 2 — Trusted-person approval** | Floats requiring an additional approval from a designated trusted person for high-value transfers (above **₹50,000**) by vulnerable cohorts (such as citizens 70+ or differently abled persons), with a 24-hour cooldown on trusted-person changes or opt-outs. |
| Regulatory *(consultation)* | **Option 3 — KYC-commensurate credits** | Floats monitoring inbound account credits against documented customer relationship and financial/KYC profile to flag anomalous mule inflows early. |
| Regulatory *(consultation)* | **Option 4 — Customer controls & kill switch** | Floats uniform digital channel on/off switches, self-set limits across UPI/cards/netbanking, an instant **emergency kill switch** locking all digital modes together, and evaluating "secure by default" disabled channels on new accounts (risking accidental self-lockouts). |
| Atlas guidance | Product & compliance teams | Track formal RBI draft or final Master Directions following May 8, 2026 feedback before hardcoding tentative consultation figures (`₹10,000`, `₹50,000`, 1-hour settlement lags) into live systems. |

## Watch-outs
- **Consultation ≠ mandate:** Product teams should design toggleable, reversible configuration hooks rather than assuming proposed thresholds will survive intact in final circulars.
- **Usability & coercion resilience:** Any future whitelist or trusted-person mechanic needs UX friction against scammer coaching during active calls.

guideDocs.title: Methodology
guideDocs.content:
The Atlas is an India-focused **reference platform first** (with candidate solutions second), not a compliance or advisory service. Each article separates **five evidence layers**: **Regulatory** (binding mandates and official guidance scoped by entity class and date), **Industry practice** (`company-reported` or `vendor-reported` engineering practices), **Community insight** (attributed firsthand public observations), **Research & academic** (narrow empirical or `arXiv` benchmark leads), and **Atlas guidance** (editorial synthesis, candidate gap controls, telemetry prerequisites, and validation caveats).

Records follow a **Ready-Reckoner** layout for quick lookup: plain-English mechanism and impact upfront, a colour-keyed **What to do** (`Basis | Owner | Action`) checklist, operational watch-outs, and a collapsed **Sources, legal scope & review history** drawer at the bottom alongside the Record Dossier and best-effort disclaimer. A citation must support the exact claim and entity class; a rule governing a bank does not automatically govern a merchant or TPAP.

**Publication gate:** Primary source check, entity-scope and effective-date check, independent editorial review, and a passing site build. A successful build is not proof of factual accuracy; every page links directly to a **Report a factual error** issue form and GitHub source editing for human corrections.

[Read the full research protocol](https://github.com/eyeinthesky6/india-fintech-risk-atlas/blob/main/docs/RESEARCH_PROTOCOL.md).

guideDocs.title: Evidence and attribution policy
guideDocs.description: How the Atlas puts reference facts first and separates Regulatory, Industry practice, Community insight, Research & academic, and Atlas guidance layers.
guideDocs.content:
India Fintech Risk Atlas is a **reference platform first**; candidate solutions come second. Every record separates verified reference facts from company practices, practitioner accounts, academic paper leads, and editorial guidance across **five evidence layers**:

## Five evidence layers

| Layer | What it means | Typical attribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Regulatory** | Regulator or scheme operator's requirement or guidance, scoped to applicable entities and dates | RBI/NPCI, document, section and date |
| **Industry practice** | Published company implementation or case study | Company and original article; `company-reported` or `vendor-reported` |
| **Community insight** | A named individual's firsthand public observation or operational lesson | Author, role, publication date and original link |
| **Research & academic** | Published empirical or academic studies (`arXiv`, workshops, benchmarks) exploring open gaps | Authors, paper ID/venue, dataset period, sample limits, and evaluation caveats |
| **Atlas guidance** | Editorial synthesis, operational gap framing, candidate controls, telemetry prerequisites, and validation guidance | Atlas synthesis, source links, caveats, and independent reviewer state |

Academic and empirical papers sit in their own **Research & academic** layer—separate from **Industry practice**, **Community insight**, and **Atlas guidance**—so narrow benchmark results are never mistaken for production adoption or binding rules, and Atlas suggestions remain clearly attributed.

An industry claim is not a regulatory obligation. A community observation is not universal proof. Research paper leads and Atlas guidance require domain validation before production use, and users should verify original primary sources before taking material action.

## How we reference others
We link to original publications and write our own concise summaries, crediting the author or company. We do not reproduce full posts, diagrams, proprietary rules or documents without appropriate rights. Attribution alone does not provide copyright permission.

[Full evidence and rights policy](https://github.com/eyeinthesky6/india-fintech-risk-atlas/blob/main/docs/EVIDENCE_LAYERS_AND_RIGHTS.md).

guideDocs.title: Contribute
guideDocs.content:
The India Fintech Risk Atlas is an independent, public-good reference platform. We catalog fraud vectors, regulatory controls, and technical operational failure modes across Indian financial products.

We have designed our platform so that **domain experts (bankers, compliance leads, fraud investigators) never have to touch GitHub or write code**, while **software engineers and researchers can contribute through standard Git workflows**.

---

## 🧭 Choose Your Contribution Path

```
                      ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
                      │   How would you like to contribute?  │
                      └──────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                                         │
                 ┌───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
                 ▼                                               ▼
   [I am a Domain Expert / Leader]                [I am an Engineer / Researcher]
   • Bank Compliance / Risk Lead                  • Open-Source Developer
   • Payment Ops / Fraud Architect                • Data & Documentation Analyst
   • Legal & Policy Scholar                       • Astro / Web Engineer
                 │                                               │
                 ▼                                               ▼
         Zero-GitHub Path                                   Git / PR Path
    (2-minute async delta reviews)                    (Task Board & Double-Ledger)
```

---

## 🏛️ Path 1: Domain Experts & Atlas Advisory Panel (Zero GitHub Required)

Most senior risk architects and banking compliance officers do not use GitHub. We guarantee that **you will never be asked to write code, resolve merge conflicts, or manage pull requests.**

### How the Zero-GitHub Review Loop Works
1. **Automated Monitoring:** Our automated watcher bots monitor RBI Master Directions, NPCI circulars, and engineering blogs daily.
2. **AI & Maintainer Drafting:** When a change occurs, an AI assistant or technical maintainer drafts a **concise 3-bullet operational summary** and table update.
3. **2-Minute Async Review:** You receive a short brief via email or WhatsApp:  
   > *"RBI has updated the timeline for customer unauthorized debit reporting under Circular X. We drafted this 1-line update to `UPI-015`. Does this reflect what your bank/PSP enforces in production?"*
4. **Attribution:** Once you confirm or tweak the note, the record is published with your attribution:  
   *`Topic Lead: [Your Name] — Head of Fraud Risk, [FinTech / Bank]`* (or anonymized as *`Senior Bank Risk Lead`* if required by your employer).

### How to Sign Up as a Domain Expert:
- **Option A (Web / Direct):** Fill out our quick [Domain Expert Registration Form](https://forms.gle/RiskAtlasExpertSignup) *(Google Form / Tally)* or email your role and domain of interest directly to `atlas@six.tech`.
- **Option B (GitHub):** If you already have a GitHub account, submit a [Domain Expert Registration Issue](https://github.com/eyeinthesky6/india-fintech-risk-atlas/issues/new?template=domain-expert-signup.yml).

### Available Domain Tracks:
- **UPI & Immediate Payments:** Real-time velocity, QR spoofing, collect requests, UDIR dispute flows.
- **Credit & Debit Cards:** CoFT tokenization failures, recurring mandates, chargeback pre-arbitration.
- **Payment Aggregators & Gateways:** Escrow management, merchant KYC, transaction laundering.
- **Digital Lending:** First-Loss Default Guarantees (FLDG), Regulated Entity (RE) oversight, recovery agent ethics.
- **Mule Accounts & AML:** Dormancy-to-burst patterns, shell company accounts, state cybercell freezing orders.
- **Mobile Security & RASP:** Screen-overlay attacks, root bypass, malicious APK detection, biometric step-up.
- **Atlas Advisory Panel:** Strategic institutional oversight, regulatory consultation memos, civil society coordination (e.g. Internet Freedom Foundation - IFF).

---

## 💻 Path 2: Code & Content Contributors (GitHub & Pull Requests)

For developers, technical researchers, and data engineers who want to add new topic records, improve scrapers, or enhance the Astro website.

### Step 1: Register Your Interest
Open a [Contributor Registration Issue](https://github.com/eyeinthesky6/india-fintech-risk-atlas/issues/new?template=contributor-signup.yml). Our welcome bot will immediately guide you to active issues and assign topic labels.

### Step 2: Pick a Work Unit
Check the live [Product Expansion Task Board](https://github.com/eyeinthesky6/india-fintech-risk-atlas/blob/main/docs/PRODUCT_EXPANSION_TASKBOARD.md). Work is organized into single, bounded work units (max 1 topic record per PR).

### Step 3: Enforce Double-Ledger Parity
Every new claim or updated row in `src/content/docs/<product>/<ID>.md` must have matching 1:1 entries in:
- `research/evidence/<ID>.md` (Claim-by-claim assertion ledger mapping to one of the 5 evidence layers: `Regulatory`, `Industry practice`, `Community insight`, `Research & academic`, or `Atlas guidance`).
- `research/attestations/<ID>.md` (12-item declaration checklist; note that contributor/author agents **cannot** self-certify reviewer boxes `8–10, 12`).

### Step 4: Run Verification Before Submitting
```powershell
# 1. Verify attestation ledgers and stage parity
python scripts/check-attestations.py --all

# 2. Verify citation freshness and check link health
python scripts/verify-citations.py --offline --all

# 3. Test website build and link integrity
npm run build
```

---

## 🔍 Report an Error or Share Live Operational Feedback

If you spotted an outdated circular, missing carve-out (e.g. Small Finance Bank vs. Commercial Bank), or broken link:

1. **On-Page Error Reporter:** Use the **Report an error** button at the bottom of any topic record to highlight specific text.
2. **Factual Correction Form:** Open a structured [Factual Correction Issue](https://github.com/eyeinthesky6/india-fintech-risk-atlas/issues/new?template=factual-correction.yml) with the primary source link.
3. **Automated Triage:** Our triage bot queues the report, notifies maintainers, and runs automated link validation.

This page synthesizes **Atlas guidance** grounded in verified **Regulatory** obligations, documented **Industry practice** patterns, **Community insight** (when verified), and empirical **Research & academic** studies. No universal thresholds or proprietary bank rule sets are asserted.

## 1. Control ownership across the UPI lifecycle

Fraud, AML, and operational failures cut across separate institutional boundaries; no single entity sees every signal:

| Lifecycle stage | Primary actors | Principal failure modes | Core controls & Atlas pages |
|---|---|---|---|
| Onboarding & app integrity | Banks, PSPs, TPAPs, PAs, acquiring banks | Rogue/repackaged apps, compromised devices, shell merchants, mule onboarding | Signed install checks, device/SIM binding ([Account takeover](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/account-takeover/)), remote-access & screen-mirroring blocks ([Untrusted apps](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/untrusted-app-access/)), PA CDD/CPV/MCC vetting ([Merchant onboarding](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/merchant-onboarding/)) |
| Initiation & intent | App, customer, merchant checkout | Misdirected pull/QR scams, deep-link tampering, social-engineering urgency | P2P collect elimination / P2M clarity ([Collect-request deception](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/collect-request-deception/)), payee verification & Signed Intent ([QR & cashback deception](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/qr-cashback-deception/)) |
| Authentication & authorization | Issuer/remitter bank, PSP, switch | Credential compromise, MITM, brute-force auth probing, session hijacking | Two-factor + dynamic authentication ([Authentication context](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/authentication-context/)), failed-auth lockout & alerts ([Failed authentication](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/failed-authentication/)) |
| Real-time & behavioral monitoring | Remitter bank, beneficiary bank, non-bank PSO | Account draining bursts, multi-hop mule funnels, post-credential-change abuse | Outbound velocity bursts ([Unusual outbound velocity](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/unusual-outbound-velocity/)), parameterized EFRM ([Transaction velocity](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/transaction-velocity/)), graph/relational mule scoring ([Mule-account funnel](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/mule-account-funnel/)) |
| Processing & fulfilment | Merchant, PA/PG, acquiring & remitter banks | Duplicate webhooks, client-callback spoofing, `PENDING` vs. settled mismatch | Signature verification, raw-body HMAC, event deduplication, order state machine ([Payment status & reconciliation](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/payment-status-reconciliation/)) |
| Settlement & clearing | Remitter bank, beneficiary bank, NPCI switch | Unmatched settlement files, delayed failed-transaction reversals | <= 24h settlement reconciliation, `T+1`/`T+5` auto-reversal TAT tracking ([Settlement exceptions](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/settlement-exceptions/)) |
| Investigation, disputes & recovery | Banks, PSPs, TPAPs, PAs, I4C/NCRP | Fragmented case context, unresolved complaints, wrongful freezes, repeat fraud | ODR tracking ([Dispute routing](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/dispute-routing/)), 24x7 reporting + NCRP/1930 linkage & value-dated reversals ([Customer protection](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/customer-liability/)) |

## 2. How engineering teams operationalize an Atlas record

Rather than treating records as compliance prose or fixed rule thresholds, use each page as an implementation checklist across five steps:

1. **Scope obligations by actor (Regulatory):** Check the page's `Actors` strip (`Remitter bank`, `PSP bank`, `TPAP`, `Payment aggregator`) and pull every non-optional RBI or NPCI mandate that applies to your license category—such as P2P collect discontinuation, daily (`<= 24h`) settlement matching, `T+1`/`T+5` auto-reversal TATs, or 24x7 unauthorized-debit reporting.
2. **Audit telemetry & event schemas first (Industry practice & Atlas guidance):** Confirm the required inputs exist and agree across systems before building detections (unique `RRN`/`UTR` and gateway event IDs, device-binding age, remote-access/screen-share flags, counterparty novelty, raw-body webhook HMAC verification state, and post-credential-change timestamps).
3. **Ship deterministic guardrails and state invariants:** Implement unambiguous deterministic checks before statistical scoring—webhook signature verification + idempotent state transitions ([Payment status & reconciliation](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/payment-status-reconciliation/)), signed QR/intent checks ([QR & cashback deception](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/qr-cashback-deception/)), device/SIM binding ([Account takeover](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/account-takeover/)), and failed-auth lockouts ([Failed authentication](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/failed-authentication/)).
4. **Calibrate candidate detections in shadow (observe-only) mode:** Measure alert volume, `precision@k` at your actual analyst queue capacity, and false-positive customer overturn rates against your own historical traffic instead of copying external cutoffs.
5. **Wire tiered actions, analyst context & feedback loops:** Route technical failures (debited/uncredited) to ODR instead of fraud queues, pass structured event context to analysts, prefer proportionate step-ups or contested-amount holds over blanket freezes, and feed delayed chargebacks/NCRP outcomes back into validation.

## 3. Prioritize deterministic foundations before complex ML

1. **Event identity & state integrity first:** Before scoring fraud, guarantee unique transaction references (RRN/UTR, order ID, gateway event ID) and accurate webhook/settlement reconciliation so failed or retried payments are never misclassified as fraud or double-fulfilled.
2. **Baseline rules & parameterized monitoring:** Under RBI digital payment security controls (`id=13642` / `id=13624` / `id=13633` §§52–53), banks already document parameterized monitoring across velocity, high-risk MCCs, new-account spikes, geo/IP anomalies, and known fraud-linked VPAs/mobile numbers.
3. **Graph & ML models only when queue geometry justifies them:** Empirical benchmarking on the RBIH NFPC dataset (`arXiv:2610.21314v1`, Research & academic lead) found that for tight daily analyst queues (`k = 100`), well-featurized gradient-boosted trees (`XGBoost`/`LightGBM`) achieved 96–99% precision, whereas deeper queues (`k = 500`) benefited meaningfully from temporal heterogeneous graph models capturing shared counterparties, addresses, and PINs.

## 4. Investigation workflows and customer-impact safeguards

Detection without disciplined case management shifts harm onto legitimate customers:

- **Queue triage & explainability:** Analysts need structured case context—account tenure, recent device/credential changes, counterparty diversity, prior NCRP/I4C hits, and reconciliation state—rather than an opaque score. (Compare Google's GPay LLM-reviewer study `arXiv:2410.19845v1` and OCBC's SHAP-narrative pipeline `arXiv:2607.17586v1` in [Operator insights](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/operator-insights/)).
- **Tiered friction over blanket account freezes:** A ~30% classifier precision (as observed in certain evaluated segments of `arXiv:2410.19845v1`) makes indiscriminate automatic freezes unviable for small merchants, seasonal sellers, and community collections. Use proportionate controls—step-up warnings, temporary hold on contested funds rather than total account blocks where legally permitted, and fast unblocking SLA—alongside mandatory natural-justice notice/reasoned-order governance for formal bank fraud classifications (`RBI/DoS/2026-27` FRM `id=13641 §6`).
- **Distinguish incident classes at intake:** Route technical failures (debited/uncredited) to ODR / `T+1`–`T+5` auto-reversal (`RBI/2019-20/67`), merchant fulfilment disputes to PA evidence workflows, and coercion/impersonation or unauthorised debits to 24x7 fraud desks + NCRP/1930 (`RBI/2026-27/167 §76G`).

## 5. Validate controls and run closed-loop operational feedback

- **Time-safe evaluation:** Prevent future leakage by enforcing strict per-account scoring cutoffs (`τ(v) <= t_seed`), tracking label maturity lags (chargebacks, NCRP reports, and seizure orders arrive days or weeks after the transaction; compare Stripe backtesting practice), and measuring **queue precision@k**, **customer friction/false-positive overturn rate**, and **missed-loss exposure**.
- **Correcting positive-unlabelled label bias:** As documented in `arXiv:2610.21314v1 §8`, treating all unflagged accounts as "confirmed legitimate" teaches undetected mule rings as normal behavior. Audit a stratified sample of cleared/unflagged alerts, track overturned freezes separately from confirmed fraud, and avoid circular self-reinforcing rules.
- **Policy & typology change triggers:** Recalibrate features and thresholds immediately after scheme or regulatory shifts (such as P2P collect discontinuation, DoT MNRL updates, or `RBI/2026-27/167` effective Jan 1, 2027).

## Evidence boundaries

**Regulatory:** entity-scoped RBI directions (`id=13642`, `id=13624`, `id=13633`, `Id=13751`, `Id=12898`, `Id=13543`, `id=12896`, `Id=11693`, `Id=11946`, `id=13641`).  
**Industry practice:** Razorpay, Cashfree, Stripe (non-India method).  
**Community insight:** None promoted on this synthesis page yet (open for verified, named submissions).  
**Research & academic:** `arXiv:2610.21314v1`, `arXiv:2410.19845v1`, `arXiv:2607.17586v1` (benchmark findings, not turnkey rules).  
**Atlas guidance:** This lifecycle architecture and 5-step operational workflow (independent review pending).

See [Operator insights](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/operator-insights/), [Glossary](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/glossary/), and [Evidence policy](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/evidence-policy/).

guideDocs.title: Operator Insights & Evidence
guideDocs.description: Company-reported payment engineering docs (Industry practice) alongside empirical Research & academic studies.
guideDocs.content:
This page separates **company-reported engineering practices** (`Industry practice`) from binding **Regulatory** mandates, named **Community insight** observations, empirical **Research & academic** studies, and **Atlas guidance**. Company docs describe how one provider integrates or operates—they are neither universal bank practices nor RBI/NPCI mandates. Academic papers sit in their own `Research & academic` layer with explicit dataset limits—never as ready-to-use bank rules.

## 1. Payment event duplication, signatures, and ordering

**Industry — Razorpay technical documentation (`company-reported`).** Razorpay explains that webhooks follow at-least-once delivery, can arrive more than once or out of order, and use a 5-second acknowledgement timeout with 24-hour exponential-backoff retries before webhook disablement. It prescribes HMAC-SHA256 verification against raw request bytes via `X-Razorpay-Signature`, atomic deduplication on `x-razorpay-event-id`, separating browser `callback_url` redirects from server-to-server webhooks, and using idempotency headers on outbound refunds/payouts. [1]

**Industry — Cashfree technical documentation (`company-reported`).** Cashfree documents verifying `x-webhook-signature` (HMAC-SHA256 over `x-webhook-timestamp` plus raw payload) before executing downstream actions, checking `x-idempotency-header` (supported on webhook versions from `2025-01-01`), and handling default delivery retries (three attempts at 2, 10, and 30 minutes). [4]

**Atlas interpretation — operational gap.** If a merchant treats each webhook HTTP call as a fresh payment event, network timeouts or retries trigger duplicate fulfilment or premature refund reversals. Separate **event intake deduplication** (unique event ID / idempotency header after signature verification) from **business-state transitions** (allowing `created → authorized → captured/paid` once per order and reconciling with settlement/status APIs).

**Data needed:** raw payload bytes, signature and timestamp headers, provider event ID, merchant order ID, gateway payment/RRN/UTR reference, durable processing log.

**Validation:** replay duplicate and out-of-order payloads in staging; reject 1-byte tampered payloads; verify single fulfilment. **False positives:** redelivery after a slow `2xx` response does not imply a second customer debit or fraud.

## 2. Checkout initiation flows: UPI Intent vs. P2M Collect

**Industry — Razorpay payment flow engineering (`company-reported`).** Razorpay differentiates mobile app-to-app deep-linking (**UPI Intent**) from manual VPA entry (**UPI Collect**), reporting fewer VPA typos and notification timeouts on mobile Intent alongside **Signed Intent** payloads to prevent deep-link tampering of amount or payee details. Razorpay also notes February 2026 NPCI guidelines restricting manual VPA input fields on mobile-native flows while retaining Dynamic QR / Collect on desktop web. [2]

**Atlas interpretation — security & reliability gap.** Unverified deep links or manual VPA entry introduce two different risks: parameter tampering in mobile redirects (mitigated by Signed Intent / backend order matching) vs. notification spoofing and high abandonment in Collect flows. Reconcile exact paid amount and payee server-side against order state rather than trusting client redirect parameters.

## 3. Merchant dispute and chargeback workflows

**Industry — Razorpay disputes documentation (`company-reported`).** Razorpay structures merchant dispute operations across phases—*Fraud* (issuer risk alert), *Retrieval* (soft information request), *Chargeback* (formal claim), and *Pre-Arbitration / Arbitration* (card-network escalation)—tracking states (`Open`, `Under Review`, `Won`, `Lost`, `Closed`) via dashboard and webhooks, where merchants either accept/refund or contest with transaction/delivery evidence. [3]

**Atlas interpretation.** Payment aggregators surface structured merchant dispute workflows, while underlying UPI interbank settlement/dispute rules flow through NPCI back-office/UDIR and RBI's ODR/TAT rules (covered in [Dispute routing](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/dispute-routing/) and [Settlement exceptions](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/settlement-exceptions/)).

## 4. Rule backtesting and analyst calibration (`company-reported`, non-India analogy)

**Industry — Stripe Radar (`company-reported`; non-India reference).** Stripe documents backtesting fraud rules against historical data (comparing fraud caught vs. legitimate sales blocked) and warns about label maturity lags (60–120 days for non-fraudulent baselines vs. recent fraud warnings). [5] *Do not transplant Stripe card rule syntax or thresholds to UPI.*

## 5. Community insight (practitioner observations)

No named practitioner observation is promoted to a verified UPI finding in v1. Any future entry requires the author's name, stated public role, publication date, canonical URL, firsthand-vs-secondhand status, and independent verification.

## 6. Research & academic studies (empirical papers — dataset limits apply)

Academic papers live in their own **Research & academic** layer because empirical studies evaluate narrow datasets or benchmarks rather than turnkey production rules:

- **RBIH NFPC Money-Mule Benchmark (India, 2026):** Using the public RBIH NFPC dataset (~237.8M rows across 96,091 Indian accounts, 2,683 labelled mules), Ahmad & Deodhar compare tabular GBDTs against temporal heterogeneous GNNs (`HeteroGraphSAGE`, `RelGNN`), showing GBDTs matched GNNs at `k = 100` daily alerts (96–99% precision) while graph models degraded less at `k = 500` (~0.676–0.680 vs ~0.562–0.564), and documenting **positive-unlabelled feedback bias** when uninvestigated mule rings sit in negative labels. [6]
- **Google Pay India UPI Scam Classification Study (2024):** Dahiphale et al. evaluate fine-tuned Gemini classifiers and an LLM reviewer-assistant on balanced/sampled GPay India splits (>88% recall at ~30% precision; mixed reviewer-reasoning fidelity: 57% exact match, 32% novel valid, 6% incorrect, <1% hallucinated). *Design takeaway:* ~30% precision cannot drive blind automated blocks without human review or low-friction step-ups. [7]
- **Explainable Mule Triage (OCBC Singapore, 2026; non-India AML reference):** Zhang et al. pair 280 features, LightGBM, TreeSHAP, and constrained LLM narratives to raise live AML analyst yield from 61% to 89%—illustrating narrative-explanation ideas for investigator triage rather than India UPI rules or CPC seizure thresholds. [8]

## References

1. Razorpay, [Payment Gateway Webhooks in India: Signature Verification, Retries and Event Logs](https://razorpay.com/blog/payment-gateway-webhooks-india/), Oct 27, 2026 (accessed Nov 23, 2026).
2. Razorpay, [UPI Intent vs Collect: Which Flow Actually Works Better in 2026?](https://razorpay.com/blog/upi-intent-vs-collect-success-rates/), Apr 9, 2026 (accessed Nov 23, 2026).
3. Razorpay Docs, [About Disputes](https://razorpay.com/docs/payments/disputes), last modified Oct 8, 2026 (accessed Nov 23, 2026).
4. Cashfree Docs, [Webhooks Overview](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/payments/online/webhooks/overview) and [Webhook Verification](https://www.cashfree.com/devstudio/preview/pg/tools/webhookVerification) (accessed Nov 23, 2026).
5. Stripe, [Radar: Rules 101](https://stripe.com/guides/radar-rules-101), international fraud reference (accessed Nov 23, 2026).
6. Ahmad, O. & Deodhar, A. (2026), [Money-Mule Detection as a Relational Learning Problem: A Study on the RBIH NFPC Dataset](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.21314v1), `arXiv:2610.21314v1` (accessed Nov 23, 2026).
7. Dahiphale, D. et al. / Google, Inc. (2024), [Enhancing Trust and Safety in Digital Payments: An LLM-Powered Approach](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.19845v1), `arXiv:2410.19845v1` (accessed Nov 23, 2026).
8. Zhang, Y. et al. / OCBC Singapore (2026), [Detection, Attribution, Narration: An End-to-End Pipeline for Explainable Money Mule Identification](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.17586v1), `arXiv:2607.17586v1` (accessed Nov 23, 2026).

**Review status:** `Industry practice` docs and `Research & academic` papers retrieved and checked 2026-11-23; independent second-reviewer verification pending.

guideDocs.title: UPI Risk Glossary
guideDocs.description: Core terms, participant roles, regulatory concepts, and operational distinctions across India's UPI ecosystem.
guideDocs.content:
Definitions below reflect verified RBI regulatory terminology (where cited) and standard engineering definitions used across the Atlas.

## Ecosystem participants

- **NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India):** Scheme operator and switch for UPI; classified as a large non-bank Payment System Operator (PSO) under RBI's non-bank PSO cyber-resilience directions (`RBI/DPSS/2026-27/475`, footnote 1).
- **Remitter (Issuer) Bank:** The bank holding the payer's account from which funds are debited. Bears primary responsibility for authentication (`RBI/2025-26/79 §9`), customer transaction alerts, and customer fraud complaints.
- **Beneficiary Bank:** The bank holding the recipient's account to which funds are credited. Critical in detecting mule-account inflows (`MuleHunter.AI`) and executing `T+1` auto-reversals when unable to credit P2P transfers (`RBI/2019-20/67`).
- **Acquiring Bank:** The bank acquiring a merchant to accept digital payments, responsible for merchant policy oversight even when a merchant is onboarded via a non-bank PA (`RBI/DPSS/2025-26/141 §14`).
- **PSP (Payment Service Provider) Bank:** A bank integrated with NPCI that connects customers or TPAPs to the UPI switch and manages VPA mapping/routing.
- **TPAP (Third-Party Application Provider):** A non-bank app interface (e.g., consumer UPI apps) operating on UPI through one or more sponsor PSP banks. Covered by RBI ODR in-app grievance rules (`RBI/2020-21/21 Annex §5.2`) and NPCI's mobile security framework (see provisional mirror `NPCI/2025-26/IS/003`).
- **Payment Aggregator (PA) vs. Payment Gateway (PG):** Under `RBI/DPSS/2025-26/141 §4(i)–(j)`, a **PA** aggregates customer funds (escrow-regulated) for merchants (`PA-Online`, `PA-Physical`, `PA-Cross Border`) and performs merchant KYC/CDD and ongoing profile monitoring (`§13`); a **PG** routes payment technology without handling funds and is outside direct PA authorisation though encouraged to follow baseline security standards (`§10(g)`).

## Payment initiation & addressing

- **VPA (Virtual Payment Address):** A human-readable identifier (e.g., `name@bank`) mapped by a PSP to an underlying bank account.
- **MCC (Merchant Category Code):** A classification code assigned to onboarded merchants (`RBI/DPSS/2025-26/141 §13(e)`). High-risk MCC shifts and anomalous activity vs. declared MCC are monitoring parameters in RBI digital payment security controls (`RBI/DoS/2026-27/411 §53`).
- **UPI Intent vs. Signed Intent:** App-to-app deep-link handoff on a user's mobile device launching a UPI app with pre-filled payment parameters. **Signed Intent** cryptographically signs the payload to prevent client-side tampering of payee or amount (see Razorpay engineering docs).
- **UPI Collect (P2P vs. P2M):** A pull-style request sent to a payer's VPA requiring PIN approval. Per browser-verified NPCI circular `NPCI/UPI/OC/220/2025-26`, **P2P** collect was discontinued beyond Oct 1, 2025; **P2M** merchant collect remains distinct (with mobile checkout manual-VPA restrictions noted by operators in Feb 2026).

## Fraud, AML & liability concepts

- **Authorised Push Payment (APP) Fraud:** A fraud in which a customer is socially engineered or coerced into authorizing a genuine payment instruction to a scammer's account (highlighted in RBI's April 2026 Discussion Paper `id=23810 §x` as the dominant modern digital payment fraud category).
- **Fraudulent EBT vs. Unauthorised EBT (`RBI/2026-27/167`):** For commercial banks (for transactions on or after Jan 1, 2027), `§4(15A)` defines **Fraudulent EBT** to include both third-party credential theft *and* transactions executed by a customer granting approval under coercion, deception, or duress; `§4(26B)` defines **Unauthorised EBT** as an EBT not authorised by the customer (including bank negligence or third-party breach). Contrast with `RBI/2017-18/15` (pre-Jan-2027 / Payments Banks baseline `id=13089`).
- **Money Mule (Mule Account):** A bank account (recruited knowingly, negligently, or unwittingly) used to receive, layer, split, or withdraw proceeds of fraud or cybercrime. Monitored via transaction/relational signals and intelligence sharing between I4C's NCRP Suspect Registry and RBIH's `MuleHunter.AI`.
- **EWS / RFA (Early Warning Signal / Red Flagged Account):** Under `RBI Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2026` (`id=13641`), EWS indicators trigger deeper fraud investigation; note that formal fraud classification requires natural-justice procedural safeguards (including a minimum 21-day Show Cause Notice and reasoned order under `§6`).
- **Device Binding & RASP:** Tying a mobile payment app registration cryptographically/logically to a specific physical handset and SIM (`RBI/DoS/2026-27/411 §68(6)`, `RBI/DPSS/2026-27/475 §31(c)`), paired with Runtime Application Self-Protection checks (root/jailbreak, debugging, screen-mirroring, and untrusted install detection).

## Operations, reconciliation & disputes

- **Event Deduplication vs. Business Idempotency:** Deduplication ignores repeated delivery of the same notification ID (`x-razorpay-event-id`, `x-idempotency-header`); business idempotency ensures a single underlying payment only fulfills or settles an order once even across out-of-order webhooks and API polling.
- **TAT (Turn Around Time) & Auto-Reversal:** Statutory outer limits under `RBI/2019-20/67` for failed UPI transactions (`T+1` for P2P credit failure; `T+5` for merchant confirmation timeout), carrying automatic `₹100/day` compensation beyond the deadline.
- **ODR (Online Dispute Resolution):** Rule-based automated dispute handling mandated by `RBI/2020-21/21` across PSOs, PSPs, and TPAP apps for failed transactions with unique tracking IDs.
- **Shadow Reversal:** Temporary/provisional credit issued by a bank to a victim's account upon notification of an alleged unauthorised/fraudulent transaction prior to completion of investigation (`RBI/2017-18/15 §9`; `RBI/2026-27/167 §4(25A)`).

## Navigation

- [UPI overview](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/)
- [Risk-stack playbook](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/risk-stack-playbook/)
- [UPI source register](/india-fintech-risk-atlas/upi/sources/)

## Browser-verified NPCI pages and circulars (checked 2026-11-23)

Automated HTTP fetchers receive **HTTP 403 Forbidden** from `www.npci.org.in` WAF protections; therefore canonical NPCI URLs were directly opened and verified via browser on 2026-11-23 (and legacy `/what-we-do/upi/product-overview` and `/what-we-do/upi/faqs` `404` routes were replaced with live canonical paths):
